sources.title: Home Fire Escape Plans
sources.supports: Residents could have less than 2 minutes to escape once the smoke alarm sounds; draw a map with all doors and windows; two ways out of every room; keep doors and windows unblocked; outside meeting place in front of the home; practice with everyone; use the test button to start the drill; high-rise and condominium steps (leave and close the door, pull the alarm, use stairs not elevator unless directed, stay at the meeting place, tell the fire department if someone is trapped).
sources.notes: Upgraded from the register placeholder. Page shows no published or updated date. Handouts and pictographs on the page were not opened.

sources.title: Avoiding Carbon Monoxide Poisoning (disaster PSA)
sources.publisher: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (National Center for Environmental Health)
sources.supports: During a power outage never use generators, grills or other gasoline-, propane- or charcoal-burning devices inside the home, garage or carport or near doors, windows or vents; CO is odorless and colorless; 'kills more than 500 Americans each year'; do not heat the home with a gas oven; keep generators at least 20 ft from doors, windows and vents; 800-CDC-INFO.
sources.notes: Upgraded from the register placeholder. The visible 'Updated' date (Nov 1, 2023) precedes the 'Published' date (May 15, 2024); both recorded as shown. The '500 a year' figure differs from the same agency's CO basics page ('more than 400', non-fire); see shelter-cdc-co-basics.

sources.title: What to Do to Protect Yourself During a Power Outage
sources.publisher: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (National Center for Environmental Health)
sources.supports: CO rules for generators (20 ft, longer extension cord, battery CO detector, never in basement, garage or enclosed structure even with doors open unless professionally installed and vented), never charcoal grills, camp stoves or lanterns indoors, never run a vehicle in a garage; never heat with a gas range or oven; CO symptoms and 911 / Poison Control 1-800-222-1222; food (4 h fridge, 48 h full freezer) and refrigerated-medication guidance; heat stroke; no air conditioning options; hypothermia below 95 F; heat sources; flashlights over candles; do not siphon gasoline.

sources.title: Carbon Monoxide (CO) Poisoning Basics
sources.publisher: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (National Center for Environmental Health)
sources.supports: CO is odorless and colorless; symptoms are flu-like; people who are sleeping or intoxicated can die before symptoms; infants, older adults and people with chronic heart disease, anemia or breathing problems more likely to get sick; more than 400 non-fire CO deaths a year; detectors near every sleeping area, check batteries when clocks change, replace per manufacturer or every 5 years; annual servicing of fuel-burning appliances and chimney; never burn charcoal or use a camp stove or flameless chemical heater indoors; generator rules; vehicle in garage.
sources.notes: Detector-placement wording differs from CPSC and Ready.gov; see the cluster notes.

sources.title: Carbon Monoxide Information Center
sources.supports: More than 200 US deaths a year from non-fire CO linked to consumer products, more than 100 of them from portable generators; one portable generator can produce as much CO as hundreds of cars; never use portable generators inside homes or garages even with doors and windows open; outside only, at least 20 ft from homes with exhaust facing away; CO alarms on every level and outside sleeping areas, interconnected best; symptoms; if suspected get outside to fresh air, then call 911.
sources.notes: No page date shown. Page is marked noindex in its metadata and carries current recall notices in its sidebar; those were not used.

sources.title: Portable Heaters & Camping Equipment
sources.supports: People die each year from CO from portable heaters, lanterns and stoves used in tents, campers and vehicles; never use fuel-burning portable heaters or lanterns while sleeping in enclosed areas; risk is higher at altitude; CO poisoning is easily mistaken for cold or flu; kerosene heaters take only water-clear 1-K grade kerosene, never gasoline.
sources.notes: No page date shown. The linked CPSC safety-alert PDFs were not opened.

sources.title: Safety Guidelines: During & After a Winter Storm
sources.publisher: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (National Center for Environmental Health)
sources.supports: Space heater rules (automatic shut-off, 3 ft clearance, never cover, no extension cords); combustion heaters only if vented outside; proper ventilation if a kerosene heater must be used; use only the fuel the heater is designed for; generator placement and cords; conserving heat; babies under one never sleep in a cold room, soft-bedding warning; older adults make less body heat; frozen pipes; hypothermia and frostbite signs; stranded-in-car steps; alcohol and caffeine.

sources.title: About Heat and Your Health
sources.publisher: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (National Center for Environmental Health)
sources.supports: Fans only when indoor temperature is under 90 F; find air conditioning via 2-1-1, cooling-center listings, health department or emergency management; hydration; symptoms of overheating; check on neighbors and pets; medicines and power outages; higher-risk groups (children, older adults, pregnancy, heart disease, asthma).
sources.notes: Fetched from https://www.cdc.gov/extreme-heat/prevention/index.html, which redirects to this URL.

sources.title: Power Outages
sources.supports: Generator and fuel outdoors at least 20 ft from windows, doors and attached garages; CO detectors with battery backup on every level; keep generator dry; heavy-duty cords; let it cool before refueling; no gas stove or oven for heat; plan for medicines and power-dependent medical devices; check local officials for heating and cooling locations; go to a community location with power if heat or cold is extreme; fridge about 4 h and full freezer about 48 h; inventory electric-dependent items.

sources.title: Extreme Heat
sources.supports: Extreme heat definition (above 90 F for two to three days); do not rely on a fan as the primary cooling device; cooling centers; cool showers; check on older adults and neighbors; heat stroke signs and response (call 911, cool the person, wet cloths or ice pack on head, neck, armpits and groin); heat exhaustion response; LIHEAP; summer-break family planning.
sources.notes: Ready.gov gives 'above 103 F' as a heat-stroke sign; CDC's power-outage page says body temperature can rise to 106 F or higher within 10 to 15 minutes. Different statements, not a contradiction, but flagged.

sources.title: Winter Weather
sources.supports: Winter storm warning, watch and advisory definitions and typical lead times; storms can cut heat, power and communications; CO detectors with battery backup; generators and grills outdoors only; never heat with a gas stovetop or oven; stay off roads; frostbite and hypothermia signs and first actions (no massage or heating pad for frostbite); LIHEAP.

sources.title: Home Fires
sources.supports: A fire can become life-threatening in two minutes; smoke alarm maintenance; two ways out of each room; windows, screens and security bars; practice in the dark; teach children not to hide from firefighters; wheelchair and walker doorways; sleep with bedroom doors closed; feel doors before opening; crawl low; what to do if you cannot get out; stop, drop and roll; portable-heater and kerosene-heater tips; never use a range or oven to heat; generators never indoors.

sources.title: Home Fire Escape Planning
sources.supports: One or two minutes to escape; alarms in every sleeping room, outside each sleeping area and on every level; floor plan with two ways out of each room; outside meeting place a safe distance in front; assign helpers for infants, older adults and people with mobility limits, with a backup; security-bar release devices; practice twice a year; check whether children wake to the alarm; escape ladders; sealing yourself in; high-rise residents may be safer defending in place; once out, stay out.
sources.notes: NFPA is a nonprofit standards and education body, not a government agency. 'regulator' is the closest allowed kind value; the lead may want a separate kind. Page shows no date.

sources.title: Smoke Alarm Information
sources.supports: Placement (every sleeping room, outside sleeping areas, every level, 10 ft from the stove); interconnected alarms; monthly testing; replace the whole unit 10 years after manufacture; meaning of three beeps, single chirp and continued chirping; alarms for people who are deaf or hard of hearing (strobes, bed shakers).
sources.notes: Nonprofit standards body, not a government agency (see shelter-nfpa-escape). The page states that working alarms cut the risk of dying in a home fire both 'by 60 percent' and 'in half'; this guide quotes neither figure.

sources.title: Shelter
sources.supports: Three meanings of 'shelter' (stay at home, mass care shelter, shelter in place); follow local authorities; mass care shelter points (bring your kit, confined space, service animals accepted, many shelters and hotels do not allow pets, text SHELTER and ZIP to 43362); sheltering in place steps and 'sealing a room' as a temporary measure needing pre-planning.

sources.title: Evacuation
sources.supports: Know your risks, destinations, zones and routes; go-bag; several destinations in different directions; pets; route may be on foot; fuel (full tank when evacuation likely, half tank at all times); one car per family; leave early; tell the out-of-state contact where you are going; leave a note; check on neighbors needing a ride; no shortcuts; after an evacuation check with officials before returning; generators outdoors only and never connected to the home's electrical system.

sources.title: Tornadoes
sources.supports: Warning actions; FEMA safe room or ICC 500 storm shelter, otherwise a small interior windowless room or basement on the lowest level of a sturdy building; cover head and neck; vehicle guidance ('no safe option'); text rather than call afterward.

sources.title: Hurricanes
sources.supports: Storm surge historically the leading cause of hurricane deaths; know your evacuation zone and leave immediately if told to in a mandatory zone; interior room or storm shelter for wind; highest level if trapped by flooding, never a closed attic; six inches and one foot of moving water; hurricanes are not just a coastal problem.

sources.title: Floods
sources.supports: Floods are the most common US disaster; flash floods can come without warning; 'depending on the type of flooding' evacuate, move to higher ground or a higher floor, or stay where you are; Turn Around, Don't Drown; never drive around barricades; stay in a car trapped in moving water and climb out only if water rises inside; highest level, not a closed attic; homeowner's policies do not cover flooding and NFIP policies typically take up to 30 days.

sources.title: Wildfires
sources.supports: Know evacuation zone and evacuate immediately when told to; plan for office, school and daycare; designate a closed-off room with a portable air cleaner for smoke; if trapped call 911 but response may be delayed or impossible; if not ordered out but smoky stay in a safe location or go to a lower-smoke community building; return only when authorities say it is safe.

sources.title: Chemicals and Hazardous Materials Incidents
sources.supports: Signs of a chemical release; some toxic chemicals are odorless; instructions differ by threat and 'sometimes it may be safer to shelter inside your home, other times it may be safer to evacuate'; evacuation, stay-indoors and outside-when-it-happens steps; do not leave shelter, even to help others, until authorities say it is safe; self-decontamination when medical help is not available.

sources.title: Make A Plan
sources.supports: Family may not be together; know how you'll contact one another and reconnect; familiar, easy-to-find meeting place; five discussion questions (alerts, shelter plan, evacuation route, communication plan, kit); household-needs checklist (ages, medical, disabilities and access and functional needs, languages, pets, school-aged children); document and practice the plan.
sources.notes: Fetched from https://www.ready.gov/make-a-plan, which redirects to this URL.

sources.title: Plan for Locations
sources.supports: Plan for the places the household goes regularly (school and daycare among them); get the organization's alerts, evacuation and shelter-in-place plans; neighbors, condominiums and apartments (who checks on elderly or disabled neighbors; backup plans for children if you cannot get home); high-rise and vehicle guidance.

sources.title: Make a Plan Form (Family Emergency Communication Plan)
sources.supports: Fields of Ready.gov's family emergency communication plan: household, family members (mobile, other number or social media, email, medical information), schools, childcare, caregivers and workplaces with hotline and pick-up plan, emergency contacts, meeting places, medical information including assistive devices; stated that information entered is not saved, stored or shared by any government agency.
sources.notes: Fetched from the old PDF address https://www.ready.gov/sites/default/files/2021-04/family-emergency-communication-plan.pdf, which now redirects to this web form; the PDF itself was not read. The page's displayed 'Last Updated' date (10/30/2026) is later than the day it was read and is probably dynamic; recorded as shown. The register placeholder ready-are-you-ready was NOT upgraded.

sources.title: People with Disabilities
sources.supports: Support network and accessible evacuation transportation; voluntary registries kept by some city and county emergency management agencies; priority power restoration lists; assistive-technology and mobility-equipment backups; guidance for people who are deaf or hard of hearing, blind or low vision, with speech or intellectual or developmental disabilities, or with Alzheimer's and dementia; extreme-heat risks for people with spinal cord injuries, certain medications, cognitive disabilities.

sources.title: Tips for Communicating in an Emergency
sources.supports: Congestion on phone networks in emergencies; limit non-emergency calls; try text messaging, which often goes through when calls do not; try multiple services; wait 10 seconds before redialing; backup power; designate an out-of-area person as central contact and make sure everyone knows who to contact; keep a corded phone that does not depend on electricity.
sources.notes: No date on the page and its disability section uses dated technology (pagers, PDAs). Used only for the general network-congestion points.

sources.title: Reunification with Children After a Disaster or Emergency
sources.publisher: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (Office of Readiness and Response)
sources.supports: Reunification defined; faster reunion gives better outcomes for children; about 69 million children are in school or childcare on a weekday; a family plan has phone numbers, emergency contacts and multiple meeting places; schools and childcare have their own plans; contact cards for school bags; help older children memorize names and numbers; learn school drill procedures from the principal; NCMEC hotline 1-800-THE-LOST; Hurricane Katrina and Rita figures.
sources.notes: The page's 'Reviewed' date (Jan 6, 2021) is earlier than its 'Published' date (Nov 15, 2024); recorded as shown.

sources.title: Reunification
sources.supports: Reunification is a slow, careful process and not a normal pick-up; one state's guidance to parents: stay home and do not rush the school, wait for the school's notification of time and place, bring photo ID and a pen, limit calls and texts to keep networks open.
sources.notes: State-specific (Colorado). Publisher taken from the site, which names itself 'The Office of School Safety'; the parent department was not confirmed. Other states and districts differ. No page date shown.

sources.title: NOAA Weather Radio All Hazards
sources.supports: NWR broadcasts official NWS warnings, watches and forecasts 24 hours a day; works with the Emergency Alert System; also carries non-weather hazard information including chemical releases; needs a special receiver; some transmitters are out of service and the county coverage listing should be checked.
sources.notes: Page shows live outage notices; no page date.
